Two-Dimensional Arrays

Stage 4 Concept ⏱ 14 min 📖 Glossary

A 2D array is a grid: rows of rows. Cinema seats, chessboards, mark tables, pixels — anything with [row][seat] addressing lives here.

🔎 Motivating questionHow do you find “block C, seat 4” without inspecting every chair in the cinema?

Objectives

  • Create grids
  • Index [row][col]
  • Loop nested rows

Needs first: Traversing and Updating Arrays

1 Start with an analogy

Real life first, code second.

The cinema. Block C, chair 4 = grid[2][3] (zero-based backstage). Some balconies are shorter — each row is its OWN array, so rows may legally differ in length (jagged).

⚠️ Where the analogy breaksWhere it breaks: cinemas label from 1 and forgive mistakes. Code labels from 0 and punishes: grid[0][0] is the true first seat, and grid[5][0] on 2 rows detonates.

2 The concept, plainly

One idea at a time, words before jargon.

Declare: int[][] g = new int[2][3]; (2 rows × 3 seats, zero-filled) or pre-filled {{1,0,1},{0,1,1}}. Read/write one seat: g[r][c].

g.length = row count; g[r].length = seats in row r — PER ROW, because jagged rows exist. Never assume all rows match.

Fill/visit with NESTED loops: outer walks rows, inner walks that row’s seats. Print rows with the print/println pattern from nested-loops.

Memory truth: there is no true “rectangle” — a 2D array is an array OF array-references. g[0] and g[1] are independent trays that happen to sit in one holder.

⚙️ Tech details — precise facts
  • Jagged arrays are normal: new int[3][] then g[0] = new int[2]; g[1] = new int[5]; — each row sized separately.
  • g.length rows vs g[r].length cols-in-that-row: using g[0].length for every row breaks on jagged grids.
  • Row swap is O(1): int[] t = g[0]; g[0] = g[1]; g[1] = t; — slips trade places, seats never move.

3 Watch it move: Cinema grid mechanics

Step at your pace. Text explains every move.

4 Live code demo

Small, correct Java 17 (LTS) code. Read, trace, copy.

Main.javaJava 17
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    int[][] seats = {{1, 0, 1}, {0, 1, 1}}; // 1 = free
    System.out.println("seat[0][1] = " + seats[0][1]);
    System.out.println("size = " + seats.length + "x" + seats[0].length);
    int free = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < seats.length; r++) {
      for (int c = 0; c < seats[r].length; c++) {
        if (seats[r][c] == 1) free++;
      }
    }
    System.out.println("free = " + free);
  }
}
▶ Output seat[0][1] = 0 size = 2x3 free = 4
  • Row 0, seat 1 reads 0 (taken).
  • Size: 2 rows × 3 seats.
  • Nested tour counts the 1s: four free.
▶️ Run it yourselfSave exactly as Main.java, then javac Main.java and java Main. Every full program in this course works this way.
💡 Why this output?Two-number addressing reads one seat; per-row lengths drive the nested count of free seats.

6 Common mistakes (at least 3)

Wrong, why, fixed — learn from realistic slips.

❌ Mistake 1: seats[3][0] on a 2-row grid.Why: Row 3 was never built — same detonation, two dimensions.
✅ Fix: Rows 0..length−1; check seats.length first.
❌ Mistake 2: Using seats[0].length for EVERY row.Why: Works until a jagged row arrives — then miscounts or crashes.
✅ Fix: Inner bound is seats[r].length, per current row.
❌ Mistake 3: One flat loop “visiting seats”.Why: A single loop visits ROWS (each an array), not seats.
✅ Fix: Nest: outer rows, inner seats[r].length.

9 Takeaways + next step

  • Grid = array of row-arrays.
  • [row][col], both zero-based.
  • Rows: g.length; seats: g[r].length per row.
  • Nested loops tour; rows may be jagged.
